articles.text: Children’s Fairyland has been celebrating for the last 75 years, and pumped up the volume with a raucous 75th birthday party on Monday, September 1. The Labor Day event drew upwards of 2,800 patrons, to enjoy and honor the establishment that has set the international standard for children’s theme parks since 1950. Throughout the day kids explored the park via Old Mother Hubbard’s shoe arch entrance, with beaming wide eyes. The party started off at 9:30 a.m. with a parade from the 19th Street BART station, with special guest DJ Lance Rock surprising the crowd by joining the march which traversed down Broadway and 21st street to the make-believe shores of Lake Merritt. articles.text: City Staff to hold public hearing on Sept. 8 The Piedmont Planning Commission will have a public hearing on Monday, September 8, at 5:30 p.m. in City Hall to consider a recommendation to the City Council to adopt the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan – a housing plan for developing City-owned land in Moraga Canyon into a new neighborhood of up to 197 multi-family housing. The controversial housing plan would provide space to develop residences of up to five stories either in the Blair Park area or on the hillside near Coaches Field. The plan includes 137 market-rate housing units and 60 low-income housing units, as well as road safety improvements and an expansion to Coaches Field. As part of the same agenda item, Monday’s planning meeting also considers a recommendation related to an Ordinance to amend City Code chapter 17, related to building height, lot frontage, and conforming revisions. Opinions on the plan’s community feedback page range from the plan being “well thought out” to concerns of wildlife endangerment and evacuation risk. “Almost all of the people who live in the district area that would be impacted by this addition of density are opposed to this plan,” writes one resident. For more information on the Moraga Canyon Housing Plan, visit piedmont.ca.gov/MCSP. To view or share comments on the plan, visit its community feedback page at https://communityfeedback.opengov.com/portals/piedmontca/Issue_14422. articles.text: The Beach Dads Club will celebrate 20 years of philanthropy this Sunday, September 7, with its popular annual Pancake Breakfast. Beach dads are preparing for an unforgettable anniversary full of new features and fun with the usual delicious flapjacks, bacon, coffee and joy starting at 9 a.m. on the Beach Elementary School playground. Rob Doebelin, this year’s Dads Club president (Padre Grande), is chomping at the bit for the big party. The Dads will soon be prepping gallons of their secret recipe to fix up a mean breakfast consisting of thousands of pancakes, countless sausage links, and more than 100 pounds of bacon. “We’re honoring Beach, our kids, and all the Padre Grandes who’ve kept this tradition alive. From stacks of pancakes to new Fun Zone surprises, to celebrating the people who make this community special — with staff, teachers, firefighters, and police eating free — we want this year’s breakfast to feel like both a thank-you and a kickoff to the next 20 years of fun, friendship, and community spirit,” said Doebelin. The MCSP calls for building 197 housing units on Moraga Ave. (either in Blair Park or on the steep hillside above and around Coaches Field.) Some of us who have followed the Plan’s development for 3 years have questions and serious concerns for Piedmont’s future if it becomes a reality. Here are a few. Disaster Evacuation: Piedmont Fire Dept. cites Moraga Canyon as a “high risk wildfire” area and predicts a wildfire is “highly likely.” The Canyon is also less than 1 mile from the Hayward Fault. Moraga Ave. is a designated emergency evacuation route and is the only way out for the estimated 400 to 1,000 new Canyon residents, as well as for many existing nearby Oakland and Piedmont residents. The Plan expects people to walk or bicycle in a disaster. How likely is that? How will emergency crews reach the Canyon if Moraga Ave. is gridlocked as residents desperately try to leave? Remember the 1991 Oakland hills fire. Does Piedmont want to risk its residents’ lives? Known Obstacles: The Plan itself acknowledges constraints to the development, stating that hydrology “could cause dangerous road conditions on Moraga Ave. during significant rain and cause local flooding.” Stormwater storage basins at both site options may have to be replaced. articles.text: As the weather turns hotter and vegetation dries out, the Piedmont Fire Department urges residents to prepare their yards for fire season by trimming trees and shrubs, clearing flammable materials, and removing dead vegetation around their property. Even if these steps were taken earlier this summer, PFD advises another round of clearing as fall nears. The East Bay hills have had significant wildfires in September and October multiple times in the last 150 years. Communities are best protected when everyone takes steps to manage the vegetation around their homes, which helps to reduce the spread and severity of fires when they start. Residents can do their part by taking a few simple protective measures in their yards every fall. The Fire Department asks residents to make time in the next few weeks to prepare their properties: Clear debris Remove all dead plants, grass, and weeds around the yard. Clear leaves and pine needles from roofs, gutters, and the ground. Remove flammable materials, such as paint or propane containers from under decks and away from buildings. Trim plants of dead material It’s important to keep all plants in the yard watered and well-maintained. Remove any dead or dying vegetation. If you have trees that shed bark or leaves such as eucalyptus in the yard, remove any shed debris. Create space between plants and home Remove branches that hang over the roof or are within 10 feet of the chimney. Prune plants away from buildings. This buffer area will help protect the house and give firefighters an area to work in to defend your home during a fire. Create space between plants Trim trees so the lowest branches are at least six feet from the ground, or three times the height of any shrubs beneath the tree. This helps prevent fire from moving from the ground to the treetops, where it can spread more quickly. Download a checklist for preparing your yard at piedmont. ca.gov/YardChecklist. Find more information and links to additional resources on preparing your property for fire season at piedmont.ca.gov/vegetation. If you need help identifying what needs to be done on your property, call the Fire Department at (510) 420-3030 to request an inspection.

articles.text: The best practice in vegetation management is to remove all vegetation within five feet of your home. Even if this is not currently feasible for you, taking protective measures in your yard will increase your home’s chance of surviving a wildfire and reduce risk to our whole community. Use this checklist to prepare your yard. CREATE SPACE Maintaining adequate space between plants, structures, and other objects on your property makes it harder for a fire to spread. Trim trees so that the lowest branches are at least 6 feet from the ground, or 3 times the height of any shrubs beneath the tree. Trim trees so that branches are 10 feet apart from other trees. Remove branches within 10 feet of your chimney. Remove branches that hang over your roof. Remove or prune plants and shrubs near windows. Move patio furniture, wood piles, etc. away from plants. CLEAR DEBRIS & FLAMMABLE MATERIAL Clear leaves, pine needles, and other debris from roofs, gutters, and the ground. Remove all dead plants, grass, and weeds around your property. Remove plant debris and other flammable materials, such as propane containers and paint from under decks. KEEP PLANTS WELL MAINTAINED Whether you have natives or non-natives, the most important thing is to keep all plants in your yard watered and well-maintained. Trim any dead or dying material from plants. Keep plants watered - especially any plants located within five feet of your home. If you have Eucalyptus trees, remove any shedding bark and leaves. Minimum Vertical Clearance: Avoid Fire "Ladders" 3X X Trim trees so the lowest branches are 3 times the height of shrubs below. For example, if a 5 foot shrub is growing near a tree, the lowest branch should be be 15 feet above it - 20 feet from the ground. We're here to help! If you have questions or need assistance, call us at (510) 420-3030. Lack of vertical space between shrubs and trees allows fire to move from the ground to treetops like a ladder, leading to more intense fires. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Piedmont City Hall will be closed on Thursday, September 4, while PG&E replaces an outdated electrical transformer as part of the City’s 911 Dispatch Center replacement project. Replacing the obsolete transformer will allow the Police Department to connect to a new, independent electrical system and backup generator, ensuring continuous operations during outages. This milestone is critical for the project, which began during summer 2024. City Hall services will be unavailable but there will be no interruption to public safety. Thursday, September 4: • Public safety services will continue uninter r upted. Police, Fire, and Dispatch functions will be powered by generator. • City Hall will be closed. Services typically received at the Planning, Building, and Public Works permit counter or the City Clerk counter will not be available by phone or email. • Power will also be out at 801 • • Magnolia, Veterans Hall, and the tot lot bathroom in Piedmont Park. Recreation Department offices at 385 Hillside Avenue will remain open. KCOM will be off the air during the outage. The online meeting video archive will remain available. articles.text: Grant Program expands to rentals The California Residential Mitigation Program (CRMP) announced today its second Earthquake Brace + Bolt (EBB) grant registration period for 2025, running from August 20 through October 1. This seismic retrofit program offers up to $3,000 for older homes, now expanding to include rentals and other non-owner-occupied residential properties. For the first time, this open registration expands eligibility to include non-primary residential properties, giving landlords and other property owners the opportunity to apply for seismic retrofit grants to strengthen woodframed homes built before 1980 with raised foundations against earthquake damage. Following the successful registration of nearly 19,000 homeowners during the January registration period, CRMP is initiating a second registration phase. With more than 1,100 eligible ZIP Codes across the state - including 303 added earlier this year - qualified homeowners can apply for grants of up to $3,000 to help cover the cost of bolting houses to their foundations and bracing crawl space walls. These seismic retrofit upgrades help to reduce earthquake damage and provide more resilient housing in high-risk areas. More than $20 million in grant funding will be available to help offset the cost of seismic retrofits. Since the 2013 EBB program launch, more than 32,500 California homeowners have received grant assistance for strengthening their homes against earthquake damage. The EBB grant program is administered by CRMP, a Joint Powers Authority between the California Earthquake Authority (CEA) and the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services (Cal OES). “Offering a second registration period this year is a valuable opportunity in helping us meet the strong demand we’ve seen for earthquake retrofit assistance,” said Janiele Maffei, Chief Mitigation Officer, California Earthquake Authority. “By opening eligibility to include non-owner-occupied residential properties, we are helping ensure more of California’s older homes, including rentals, can be strengthened against earthquake damage. Retrofitting is one of the most effective ways to reduce the risk of severe damage in a major quake, protecting both residents and the communities they call home.” Income-eligible homeowners may also qualify for supplemental grants. Up to $7,000 in additional grant funds are available for households with an annual income at or below $89,040, which may provide up to 100% of the funds needed to cover a seismic retrofit. Grants are contingent upon meeting eligibility requirements and available funds. “Earthquake retrofits create a safer and more resilient California. Expanding retrofit grants to rental properties means CRMP will provide even greater protection for California’s housing stock and the families who call these properties ‘home,’” said Tom Welsh, Chief Executive Officer of the California Earthquake Authority. “Each retrofit brings us one step closer to a better-prepared California.” Beginning August 20 and running through October 1, 2025, eligible homeowners can register for a retrofit grant at EarthquakeBraceBolt.com, where they can also find detailed program information, select a trained California-licensed general contractor and view the full list of ZIP Codes and program areas. About Earthquake Brace + Bolt (EBB) Established by the California Residential Mitigation Program, EBB offers up to $3,000 to help California homeowners retrofit their house to reduce potential damage from earthquakes. A residential seismic retrofit makes a house more resistant to earthquake activity, such as ground shaking and soil failure, by bolting the house to its foundation and adding bracing around the perimeter of the crawl space. For more information, please visit: EarthquakeBraceBolt.com. About the California Residential Mitigation Program (CRMP) CRMP was established in 2011 to help Californians strengthen their homes against damage from earthquakes. CRMP is a joint powers authority created by the California Earthquake Authority and the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services. For more information, please visit crmp.org.

articles.text: More than 100 girls, parents, and siblings gathered at Beach Playfield in Piedmont for another successful Try It Out Tuesday event on August 23. The free event, coordinated by the Recreation Department’s Eva Phelan, continues to offer Bay Area girls+ the opportunity to explore new sports in a supportive and inclusive environment, with a focus on empowering girls through athletics. This month’s session gave participants the chance to rotate through three different stations: powerlifting, golf, and pickleball. Preston Pinckney of Ace Golf provided hands-on swing instruction, while members of the Piedmont Pickleball Group introduced the rules and fundamentals of their fast-growing sport. At the ever-popular powerlifting station, Piedmont High School seniors Robyn Kim and Layth Haddawy guided girls through beginner-friendly deadlifts and squats, “It looked so heavy, but it really helping many to try the sport for the first time. Kim, the 2025 U.S. National Powerlifting Champion, demonstrated powerlifting to a large audience of young female athletes at last spring’s Play It Like a Girl+ event and said she was excited to return for another opportunity to inspire girls in the community. “When I first started lifting, I didn’t see many girls in the sport,” she explained. “Now I get to show them that being strong and powerful is part of playing like a girl. Acts of Kindness as Play 15–60 min Bake cookies for neighbors; plant a tree Serenade a stranger (with consent!); dress up and deliver silly compliments on a “compliment walk” Daily Life Turned Playful Variable Grocery store scavenger hunt; car karaoke Speak in accents during errands; play “freeze dance” in the living room while folding laundry Whimsy & Absurdity 5–30 min Silly faces contest; tell jokes Hug a tree; talk to furniture; “taste a leaf”; invent a secret family handshake with five ridiculous moves Bigger Time Investments (Half Day) 2–4 hrs Picnic in the park; visit a local museum Random destination adventure (flip a coin at each intersection); “Yes Day” (kids plan everything, within reason) If you give it space, you’ll find it flows easily — whether through board games, kitchen dance parties, or off-the-wall experiments. A Menu of Fun That’s where the Family Play Menu (see table) comes in. Think of it as a “shopping list for fun.” The table offers normal options — like puzzles, nature walks, or bike rides — alongside whimsical choices that spark laughter and surprise: inventing a nonsense holiday, talking to trees, or trying the “Magic 8-Ball of Fate,” where slips of paper dictate the next random, silly challenge. It doesn’t matter which you pick. What matters is making space for play — both the ordinary and the absurd. One creates comfort and connection; the other jolts us into laughter we’ll remember years later. Why Families Need Play Now Family life today runs fast. Parents juggle work, carpools, and endless logistics; children navigate school, screens, and constant structure. Play is what interrupts that treadmill, what reminds everyone that life isn’t only about the next task or achievement. Shared play gives families breathing room, a spark of connection, and a memory that lasts far longer than the Tuesday evening routine. Lightly Through Life As the school year takes over, play isn’t something to grow out of. It’s something to grow into. Shaw’s reminder rings true, but play can also be a way of being — a lighter way of moving through the ordinary days. So this week, schedule 20 minutes of play. Be whimsical. Be ordinary. Be together. Normal life will keep its routines without you for half an hour. And as Peter Pan warned, “Once you’re grown up, you can never come back.” But perhaps you can — not to childhood itself, but to the spirit of it, carried lightly into the present. articles.text: The SAT has been administered in a digital format since last year. It is taken by millions of students worldwide as part of the college application process. At Piedmont High School, more than 120 students sit for the exam each year. The test is divided into four sections, two in reading and two in math, and typically lasts about two hours. Along with the ACT, the SAT remains a key factor for colleges that require standardized testing and can significantly influence admissions outcomes. This year, the SAT exam on August 23 proved to be one of the most chaotic yet. With over 30 PHS students testing that day, it’s no surprise that the San Francisco test centers, where most Bay Area juniors and seniors choose to take their exams, were packed with thousands of students. Students driving into San Francisco quickly found themselves stuck in standstill traffic as tens of thousands of cars clogged the streets. In fear of being late to the SAT, some students abandoned their rides altogether, sprinting along streets and weaving through red-light intersections. When they finally reached their test sites, they were met with crowds of students just like themselves, spilling across sidewalks and entryways. At the Moscone Center alone more than 4,000 students were crammed inside, facing unprepared staff and mounting confusion. What made the experience even more overwhelming was the crowd of parents pressed against the glass outside and the airport-like atmosphere inside. After half an hour of confusion, students were funneled into halls that had been hastily divided into sections. While most students were eventually able to take the exam without major issues, some areas faced Wi-Fi failures that left students sitting at their desks for hours, scrolling on their phones, only to be told they would not be able to test at all. PHS senior Mina Dao-Hoang was unable to take the August SAT due to Wi-Fi issues. “It took an hour and a half to sit down, and only a few could use Wi-Fi so they started, but the rest of us were talking and seated. People had phones out to text their parents but we could only leave around 11:30 after not being able to take it.” she said. Dao-Hoang was one of more than 600 students who never got the chance to test, and one of a few from PHS. When asked how she felt about the situation, she explained, “I didn’t study, but I can imagine that if people did, they would be really mad. The SAT is important because more schools are requiring it and if you do well, you have a higher chance to get into a prestigious school. We basically lost the opportunity to take both an August and a September SAT before college applications.” Senior Elena O’Connell, on the other hand, was able to complete the exam, but the disruptions still weighed on her. “It felt different than the other SAT I took because there were a lot more people. While you were taking the test you could hear the other proctors from the other sections through the speakers, so it was hard to focus,” said O’Connell. For both students, and for many others across the Bay Area, the August SAT may have taken away what should have been a crucial opportunity to get ahead in the college application season. The biggest update for those who were unable to test is that they now have to go out of their way to retake it this Saturday at Union Square in San Francisco. “I’m going to have to take it and then the September one in two weeks,” Dao-Hoang noted. For students already overwhelmed by the pressures of college applications, the chaos of this year’s August SAT only added another layer of stress to an already high-stakes process. Evolette Mak is a senior at Piedmont High School and an intern writer with the Piedmont Post.

articles.text: Earlier this summer, 37 eighth grade students capped off their time at Piedmont Middle School with a parent-led trip to Yosemite National Park that was organized by Judy Lin and Michelle Abernathy. As Chief Operating Officer of NatureBridge, a non-profit that runs outdoor schools in national parks, Judy uniquely understands the power of outdoor education. Michelle is a former teacher who took her students to NatureBridge and is also a mom and wife to NatureBridge alums. “We’re passionate about outdoor ed. Great things happen when students are learning out in nature together and we wanted our kids to have that experience with their classmates. Michelle and I knew we wanted to make a NatureBridge trip happen,” said Judy. What began as an idea last fall became a reality in early June as a busload of rising ninth graders and parent chaperones arrived in Yosemite Valley for their weeklong program. The trip leaders organized everything from travel logistics to finances and chaperone support to make their vision for the trip come true. The result was an unforgettable outdoor adventure. Led by NatureBridge educators, the students hiked miles around Yosemite Valley, learned Thirty-seven recent Piedmont Middle School graduates in front of Half Dome science, and got to know their classmates through team building activities. The kids challenged themselves and gained confidence throughout the week, from crawling through narrow caves to wading in cold rivers to completing their challenge hike to the top of the Mist Trail in 95 degree heat. Ben McMurtry reflects, “I liked exploring with my friends and doing cool team building activities. Not having phones meant we could do all kinds of other stuff together.” Henry Van Den Bos and his trailmates try to figure out the team challenge. A team-building exercise included being blindfolded to learn about trust and communication. Zayda Weber leads the group in a closing campfire activity.

Most students knew each other before the trip, but this shared outdoor experience that included sleeping in tent cabins and mixed trail groups allowed for wider and deeper connections. Penelope Hopper says, “Being in a different environment with people I normally see at school was definitely a bonding experience. The success of this first eighth grade trip has inspired plans for more. Judy and Michelle hope to make this trip a tradition for younger siblings. “Meaningful experiences in nature are more important than ever for kids. This trip will hopefully be something that our kids and their classmates will always remember about middle school,” said Judy. Whitney at 14,505 feet, the highest The group entered at the Cottonwood Lakes trailhead in the John Muir Wilderness at 10,000 feet, each night ascending to higher alpine lakes, including Long Lake at 11,200 feet and Guitar Lake at 11,500 feet. After ascending to New Army Pass at 12,300 feet, the group joined the Pacific Crest Trail and John Muir Trail in Sequoia National Park to reach Mt. Whitney. On the morning of the summit attempt, scouts broke camp at 5 am and started their 3,000- foot ascent in the dark lit by headlamps. As the sun rose, the scouts hiked the ridgeline below the peak, navigating exposed ledges, fields of snow, and technical traverses. articles.text: It was a tough matchup against Salesian to start Piedmont’s football season on Saturday, August 30 in Richmond, losing 41-17. Despite the defeat, the Highlanders kept things close through three quarters and trailed by just four-points with 8:08 left. The Pride also beat Piedmont last year 46-14 and returned some of their top talent, like receiver Carlton Perrilliat and running back Tyler Sadler. “It felt like last year, when we had a lead on them. But you have to play four quarters of football and your true colors show up in hard times,” said Piedmont coach Jordan Seiden. “I don’t care about the score, I care about the effort. We need to give ourselves our best chance through effort.” For a while, it looked like Piedmont was punching well above its weight class with an almost entire new roster on offense, defense, and special teams. Trailing 28-17, the Highlanders were driving downfield to Salesian’s 29, but a blown assignment led to an interception and quick score by the Pride. “Yeah, we’re a new team, but the other team doesn’t care about that. We had a missed assignment and that led to the interception,” Seiden said. Despite the disappointing result, there were some bright spots as Piedmont went up against last year’s Div. 5 North Coast Section No. 2 seed and eventual semifinalist. Sophomore quarterback Jimmy Lagios didn’t shy from the moment, looking poised navigating the pocket to elude pressure and rolling out to find receivers. Lagios connected with two teammates for touchdowns. Hurwitz, who led last year’s JV team in scoring, had an impressive 53-yard touchdown after fighting through two defenders. George Saunders scored a 25-yard touchdown, breaking a tackle on his way to the end zone. “Jimmy stepped up and played as good a game as we could ask. He was scrambling and made some plays. He got the ball out and our receivers made some nice plays. The great side of things is [that] young guys stepped up,” Seiden said. Piedmont will travel 100 miles to Middletown in Lake County for a game on Friday, September 5. Last year, PHS beat the Mustangs 42-21 at Witter Field. The Pride added another touchdown with 4:19 left in the second quarter to go up 14-0. Piedmont assumed possession at its own 47-yard line after a failed onside kick. On 3rd-and-10, Lagios hurled a ball downfield to Hurwitz, who athletically fought off pass interference and two defenders to turn up field and score with 3:51 left in the second quarter, making it 14-7. Salesian scored on their ensuing possession with 1:03 left. PHS drove 60 yards in the remaining time, including a 26 yard reception by Jack Meyjes and an 11 yard catch by Saunders. articles.text: Piedmont High’s flag football team opened up its season with a 27-6 loss to St. Mary’s on Thursday, August 28 at Witter Field. Despite the loss, there were still bright spots as Piedmont adjusts to the sport’s new rules. “That was the best loss we ever had. We started out focused and they adjusted. As the game went on, we were still energized and excited about how we played. Of course, you want to win, but we’re still feeling very positive,” said coach Beth Black. Sophomore quarterback Edie Elmquist did well, using her speed to break the pocket for rushing yards, while also finding open targets when rolling out. “Edie was phenomenal on the run; she’s utilizing her speed. She knows every route and has the confidence to dance back there. She’s showing confidence,” Black said. Senior safety Dahlia Osman also made an impact, recording two interceptions, including one in the end zone. “Dahlia is Dahlia; she’s a force back there,” Black said. Piedmont scored the final touchdown of the game when Malia Williams ran the ball 25 Staff Photos Edie Elmquist lines up for a pass in Piedmont’s second opener against St. Mary’s. yards into the end zone. Black discussed some of the work that needs to be done. “We’re going to work on flag pulling from the outside hip. We want to work on screen blocking, and just building more connections on the field,” Black said. The Highlanders look ahead to hosting Miramonte tomorrow, Thursday, September 4. Five days later, PHS opens its league schedule in the Shoreline Division of the Western Alameda County Conference against Tennyson on September 9. Dahlia Osman makes one of her two interceptions. Piedmont celebrates Malia Williams’ (middle) touchdown. Game Recap After Piedmont went threeand-out on the first possession, Saint Mary’s drove 43 yards on three plays to go up 6-0 with 8:40 left in the first quarter following a failed extra point conversion. On the next drive, Elmquist had a completion to Cory Minor while Elmquist also broke runs of five and 12 yards. However, PHS elected to punt on 4th-and-5 at their 35 yard line. After two trades of possession, Saint Mary’s drove to the 21 yard line, but Osman thwarted their series by nabbing an interception. The Panthers got the ball back with 11:15 to go in the second quarter, driving 33 yards to the end zone—making it 13-0 with 7:22 left. Piedmont’s next drive featured a 15 yard reception by Kaylani Spieckerman and a 10 yard carry by Elmquist, but the drive stalled out two yards past midfield at the St. Mary’s 38 with 26 seconds left in the half. In the third quarter, Osman had a critical takeaway by grabbing her second interception, this time jumping a route in the end zone with 4:34 on the clock. However, Piedmont’s offense punted after three plays, leading to another St. Mary’s score with 39 seconds left—19-0. The Panthers later forced a safety in the fourth quarter with 6:52 remaining in the game, 21-0. Piedmont got on the board late after just three plays. It featured Anjali Bowers recording a nine yard reception before Williams took a carry 25 yards to the house. NEXT UP Piedmont (0-1 overall) hosts Miramonte on Thursday, September 4 at 7:30 p.m. They also host Tennyson on Tuesday, September 9 at the same time.

articles.text: Photos by Jenni Tsoi Leighton Mand, the Post’s Sophomore of the Year in 2024 is back for her junior season. Piedmont High’s cross-country team returns to action this week at St. Mary’s College in Moraga on Saturday, September 6 at the St. Mary’s Invitational. They’ll compete with 31 other schools, with many teams from the North Coast Section. It’s shaping up to be a potentially strong season for the girls’ squad, led by returning runners, Leighton Mand and Amalia Gray. Both reached last year’s CIF State Championship. The Post named Mand its 2025 Sophomore of the Year following her cross country and track campaigns. She finished 74th of 201 athletes at the State Championship, while she was sixth of 127 at the NCS Championship. “Leighton is a cornerstone runner of the girls’ team. She’s consistent and competitive. She wants to work hard and race hard. She’s also shown she can look out for other members of the team,” coach Steve Zirkelbach said. Gray was among last year’s breakout stars as a sophomore as well. She was 101st at State and finished 14th at NCS. Alongside Gray and Mand, Piedmont has a very strong group of eight runners who could all make an impact. Skylar Best enters her senior year, while sophomores Viviane Oesterer and Nikita Gorelik also made an impact in their debut in 2024. Senior Cora Chun, senior Mara Kemp-Malone, and junior Cora Brozowski Schrader are three runners who should help. “Skylar is a senior and one of our captains and Amalia went to the State meet last year. Viviane is a sophomore and was one of our top runners last year at the WACC Championship and North Coast. Cora Chun is another senior captain, Cora Brozowski Schrader is looking strong as well. Nikita had a really strong track season, I’m looking forward to her being in the running,” Zirkelbach said. In total, Zirkelbach sees a girls’ group who could potentially make it to State if all goes well. “The girls look very promising if everyone can stay healthy. They have a shot to possibly make it to the State meet,” Zirkelbach. The boys’ will have to go much of the season without star runner Sebastien Swain, who underwent surgery over the offseason on a lingering injury. He was our 2025 honorable mention for Athlete of the Year. the Post’s’ first boys’ sophomore to do so. Zirkelbach is hopeful Swain can recover in time for the 2025 Western Alameda County Conference Championship near the end of the season. “Sebastien had surgery early in the summer. He’s back doing easy rehabilitation running. He’s easing back into it, and we’re hoping he can be back by the WACC Championship,” Zirkelbach said. Zirkelbach named junior Alex Schleuning as someone who is doing well, and senior Noah Sohn Amalia Gray was a breakout star as a sophomore, reaching last year’s CIF State Championship.

pages.text: Wednesday, September 3, 2025 13 Flag football drops opener to St. Mary’s By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s flag football team opened up its season with a 27-6 loss to St. Mary’s on Thursday, August 28 at Witter Field. Despite the loss, there were still bright spots as Piedmont adjusts to the sport’s new rules. “That was the best loss we ever had. We started out focused and they adjusted. As the game went on, we were still energized and excited about how we played. Of course, you want to win, but we’re still feeling very positive,” said coach Beth Black. Sophomore quarterback Edie Elmquist did well, using her speed to break the pocket for rushing yards, while also finding open targets when rolling out. “Edie was phenomenal on the run; she’s utilizing her speed. She knows every route and has the confidence to dance back there. She’s showing confidence,” Black said. Senior safety Dahlia Osman also made an impact, recording two interceptions, including one in the end zone. “Dahlia is Dahlia; she’s a force back there,” Black said. Piedmont scored the final touchdown of the game when Malia Williams ran the ball 25 Staff Photos Edie Elmquist lines up for a pass in Piedmont’s second opener against St. Mary’s. yards into the end zone. Black discussed some of the work that needs to be done. “We’re going to work on flag pulling from the outside hip. We want to work on screen blocking, and just building more connections on the field,” Black said. The Highlanders look ahead to hosting Miramonte tomorrow, Thursday, September 4. Five days later, PHS opens its league schedule in the Shoreline Division of the Western Alameda County Conference against Tennyson on September 9. Dahlia Osman makes one of her two interceptions. Piedmont celebrates Malia Williams’ (middle) touchdown. Game Recap After Piedmont went threeand-out on the first possession, Saint Mary’s drove 43 yards on three plays to go up 6-0 with 8:40 left in the first quarter following a failed extra point conversion. On the next drive, Elmquist had a completion to Cory Minor while Elmquist also broke runs of five and 12 yards. However, PHS elected to punt on 4th-and-5 at their 35 yard line. After two trades of possession, Saint Mary’s drove to the 21 yard line, but Osman thwarted their series by nabbing an interception. The Panthers got the ball back with 11:15 to go in the second quarter, driving 33 yards to the end zone—making it 13-0 with 7:22 left. Piedmont’s next drive featured a 15 yard reception by Kaylani Spieckerman and a 10 yard carry by Elmquist, but the drive stalled out two yards past midfield at the St. Mary’s 38 with 26 seconds left in the half. In the third quarter, Osman had a critical takeaway by grabbing her second interception, this time jumping a route in the end zone with 4:34 on the clock. However, Piedmont’s offense punted after three plays, leading to another St. Mary’s score with 39 seconds left—19-0. The Panthers later forced a safety in the fourth quarter with 6:52 remaining in the game, 21-0. Piedmont got on the board late after just three plays. It featured Anjali Bowers recording a nine yard reception before Williams took a carry 25 yards to the house. Photo by JC Curran Piedmont’s JV football team came away with a narrow 12-6 victory at Salesian Prep to open its season on Saturday, August 30 in Richmond. The team entered its season with 18 freshmen, eight sophomores, and three juniors who knew they had a lot of talent but hadn’t yet seen how it translated in a real game. Piedmont’s offensive line gave quarterback Jonah Cha-Foster enough time to find his receivers as he finished the game with two passing touchdowns, one to Mason Gray, and another to Mateo Long, who made a diving catch in the end zone for the catch. Cha-Foster finished the day with 100 passing yards, as well as another 40 yards on the ground. After a strong first half, Piedmont had a shaky start to the second half, giving up an onside kick which immediately resulted in a Salesian touchdown on a 40-yard carry. It seemed to cause some nerves from Piedmont after nearly relinquishing an onside kick, but the Pride was penalized for illegal touching. Piedmont went on a long drive on the ensuing possession but ultimately turned the ball over on downs at Salesian’s 12-yard line. When Salesian got the ball back, Piedmont forced a turnover on downs but failed to take advantage. With four minutes left in the game, Salesian regained possession. With two minutes left and Salesian threatening to score, outside linebacker Cyrus Emanuelson read the quarterback’s eyes to snatch an interception and secure Piedmont’s Week 1 victory. Additional key players in this game included running back-linebacker Vaja Mafi who had some explosive rushing plays on offense as well as some bruising tackles on defense. Tight end Jed Gilbert also had a good game securing a couple of catches and making effective blocks to help open up run lanes. articles.text: It was a difficult second match of the season for Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team, falling 7-0 to University in Golden Gate Park in San Francisco. Despite the one-sided score, Piedmont had some close matches throughout the day. No. 4 singles starter Arianna Kortum took University’s Lauren Connor to three sets, with each set only separated by two games or less. No. 3 doubles team Ella Thomasson and Chiara Silvo also took their match to three sets, while both of Kate Jumper’s sets at No. 2 singles were separated by two games. “We did have a few close matches. Arianna Kortum, and Ella Thomasson and Chiara Silvio each went to the deciding 10-point breaker, ”said coach Jim Landes. Thomasson and Silvo are both sophomores and new varsity starters. The duo played together as freshman last year. “Chiara and Ella played together last year. They play very well together. There’s a chance that they can move up in the lineup, but they are good at No. 3. Chiara has a nice serve and Ella can swing well too,” Landes said. The Highlanders look ahead to a match at Campolindo today, September 3, in Moraga. One day later they will travel to Dominican University in San Rafael to play Marin Academy. articles.text: Historic House and Gardens launch fall festivities Sept. 22 Fall activities are coming to Filoli this month. Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside ends its Summer Night events on September 18, and ushers in seasonal autumn festivities beginning September 22. Summer Night events include guided hikes on select evenings, live music and performances, a selection of rotating food vendors and after-hours estate access. Filoli closes its grounds at 5 p.m., but on Wednesdays and Thursdays through September 18, visitors can explore the historic house and gardens well into the evening. Located 30 miles south of San Francisco and nestled at the foot of the Santa Cruz Mountains, the scenery provides for an idyllic backdrop to view the setting sun on a pleasant summer evening. Filoli will then launch its popular lineup of fall activities, beginning with ‘Filoli Fall Tea’ on September 22. Guests are invited to a cozy afternoon tea seating in the serene Garden House, featuring seasonal ingredients and festive fall decor. A kid-friendly companion event, entitled ‘Witches Tea,’ begins October 3. Kids can snack on sweet treats and taste ‘bubbly brews’ while enjoying storytime readings. Accompanying adults get a complimentary drink with ticket purchase. The estate will revive its ‘Nightfall’ series of events on October 3, transforming the house into a haunted mansion and the gardens into a pumpkin-filled wonderland. These halloween-based events return after a successful launch last year. “Our Nightfall event offers a unique way to experience the enchanting beauty of Filoli after dark,” said Kara Newport, CEO and President of Filoli. “We look forward to welcoming families, couples, and friends to immerse themselves in this magical Halloween celebration.” Beginning October 18, estate guests will have the opportunity to taste harvested products from local vendors. A marketplace of artisans will be stationed in Filoli’s outdoor Woodland Court, where ticket holders can sample ciders, wines, handcrafted pies, jams and jellies and more. For more information and Summer and Fall activities, visit Filoli at https://filoli.org/. ®

articles.text: The 2025 World Arts West Dance Festival returns for its third and final weekend at Tunnel Tops in the Presidio in San Francisco this Sunday, September 7. The festival’s finale includes live dance perfor mances, hands-on workshops and family-friendly activities, and is free to attend. This year’s festival theme is “Dance as Health and Healing,” and features performances by Dimensions Dance Theater, one of Oakland’s most iconic Black dance companies, as well as Alleluia Panis/ KULARTS, which will present “Lakbai Diwa,” a Filipino diasporic spirit cultural ceremony and living dance prayer. The event concludes with a Haitian dance workshop hosted by Laurie Fleurentin, who will share the role of music and dance in Haitian culture. “This year we close the gap between artists and audience members where the public gets to create, move and sing right along with the artists,” Andréa Spearman, Associate Programs and Community Engagement Manager of World Arts West, said in a press release. “They get to leave with something tangible.” This is the fourth year the Presidio has hosted World Arts West, and this finale is expected to bring together a diverse community of attendees, artists, and families from across the Bay. “We are honored to welcome World Arts West back to the Presidio,” added Aya Tacdol, Community Partnerships Manager at the Presidio Trust. “The festival shares the richness of global dance traditions and reinforces our shared commitment to making the Presidio a welcoming, inclusive space for all.” The festival begins at 1 p.m. and concludes at 4 p.m. Advance registration is not required. For more information, visit https:// www.worldartswest.org/. articles.text: The Asian Art Museum in San Francisco is hosting an artist talk with Korean-Canadian playwright Ins Choi, director of the play Kim’s Convenience, on Thursday, September 11. Choi’s award-winning comedy drama Kim’s Convenience opens at American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.) on September 18. The play is based on Choi’s experiences working at his own family’s convenience store, Kim’s Grocer, in Scarborough, Toronto, and follows family patriarch Mr. Kim as he faces a changing neighborhood landscape and the gap between his values and those of his Canadian-born children. Choi called the play a “love letter to his parents and to all first-generation immigrants who call Canada their home.” Kim’s Convenience debuted on July 6, 2011 at the Toronto Fringe Festival to wide critical acclaim and inspired a popular Netflix series of the same name. Choi, creator of the play and Artist Ins Choi the Netflix show inspired by it, will be in conversation with Pam MacKinnon, Artistic Director for American Conservatory Theater, in a limited-seating discussion. MacKinnon said she is “thrilled to be bringing Ins Choi, as playwright and actor, in his beautifully crafted and deeply personal prodigal son story Kim’s Convenience to A.C.T.” Seating is first-come, firstserved, and general admission ticket purchase is required. The event begins at 6 p.m. For more information, visit https://calendar.asianart.org/ event/artist-talk-with-ins-choi/.

articles.text: San Francisco Opera’s 103rd season opens this Friday, September 5 with the company’s annual opera ball, featuring Music Director Eun Sun Kim conducting Verdi’s Rigoletto. A revival of Verdi’s masterpiece is running September 5 through 27 at the War Memorial Opera House in San Francisco. Baritone Amartuvshin Enkhbat stars as the tormented titular character Rigoletto and Romanian soprano Adela Zaharia sings Gilda, with Yongzhao Yu making his San Francisco Opera debut as the Duke of Mantua. Mezzo-soprano J’Nai Bridges stars as Maddalena and bass Peixin Chen takes on the role of Sparafucile. The cast also includes Aleksey Bogdanov (Monterone), Stella Hannock (Giovanna), Olivier Zerouali, Samuel White, Jongwon Han, Caroline Corrales, and Elisa Sunshine. Jose Maria Condemi directs Rigoletto with sets inspired by the surrealist paintings of Giorgio de Chirico. Conductor and historian Jessica Bejarano will present an introduction to Rigoletto an hour before curtain at each performance. Music Director Kim will host a talkback after a September 21 matinee performance. San Francisco Opera’s annual ball, the company’s biggest fundraiser, kicks off the 2025-26 season on September 5, held at both City Hall and the War Memorial Opera House with proceeds benefiting the artistic initiatives of San Francisco Opera and San Francisco Opera Guild’s education programs. Guests will be greeted with a festive cocktail reception followed by a dinner crafted by local chefs served in San Francisco City Hall’s rotunda. The opening night performance of Verdi’s masterpiece Rigoletto closes out the evening. The opening weekend celebrations continue on Sunday, September 7 when Kim conducts the orchestra at Golden Gate Park, featuring stars from the fall season for the popular Opera in the Park concert, now in its 50th year. Opera subscriptions and single tickets for concerts this year are available at (415) 864-3330 and sfopera.com. Opera ball tickets may be purchased online at https://www.sfopera.com/seasons/opera-ball/. articles.text: Shotgun Players presents the world premiere of Christopher Chen’s The Motion, playing at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley on September 13. Obie Award–winner Christopher Chen, the playwright, blurs the line between performance and participation in his newest play The Motion, where a heated debate slips down a kaleidoscopic ‘rabbit hole’ engaging audience members as voyeurs and accomplices. Theater guests are given voting cards and are invited to take part in the experience as it happens on stage. The Motion is a unique play that entwines clever comedy, sharp dialogue, and science fiction to create a fractal pattern of moral dilemmas. “The Motion, which riffs on the debate format before spinning into different worlds, is one of the most ambitious plays I’ve written,” said Chen. “There’s a particular thrill when you feel yourself being swayed from one side to another then back again, because it feels like you’re activating the deepest part of your humanity,” he continues. “It’s like a Russian nesting doll. You open one and there’s another inside… It’s one surprise after another,” added Shotgun Players Director Patrick Dooley. “A dominant theme that emerges in this story aligns with others that are addressed in the season, which is, what it means to be human.” The cast includes Erin Gould as Moderator/Jack Donovan, David Sinako as Dr. Alan James, Erin Mei-Ling Stuart as Dr. Sarah Matthis, Soren Santos as Professor Neel Serrano and Gabrielle Maalihan as Professor Lily Chan. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit https://shotgunplayers.org/show/the-motion/. Playbill cover for Christopher Chen’s The Motion, premiering on the Ashby Stage on September 13

articles.text: Play leaves theater next Saturday San Francisco Playhouse’s production of My Fair Lady, based on the film adaptation of George Bernard Shaw’s 1913 play Pygmalion, leaves the theater next Saturday, September 13. Single-day tickets for showtimes Tuesday through Sunday are available online now. My Fair Lady originally premiered on Broadway in 1956, telling the story of Eliza Doolittle, a Cockney flower girl who is given speech lessons from Professor Henry Higgins, a phonetician, so that she may pass as a lady. The legendary original production received unanimous glowing reviews since its opening and won six Tony Awards, including Best Musical. It ran for 2,717 performances, the longest-running musical in Broadway history at the time. The musical features a beloved score including classic songs “I Could Have Danced All Night,” “Get Me to the Church on Time,” “Wouldn’t It Be Loverly,” “On the Street Where You Live,” “The Rain in Spain,” and “I’ve Grown Accustomed to Her Face.” The score of My Fair Lady was among the most successful ever to emerge from the American musical theatre with more than five million copies of the Broadway-cast recording sold. San Francisco Playhouse’s production is directed by Artistic Director Bill English, with music direction by Dave Dobrusky and choreography by Nicole Helfer. The ensemble in4cludes Jillian Smith as Eliza Doolittle and Adam Magill as Henry Higgins, with Julio Chavez, Heather Orth, Jill Slyter, Jura Davis, Kareem Jenkins and Andy Collins rounding out the ensemble. The show is on stage six days a week; Tuesday through Sunday. For showtimes and to purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfplayhouse.org/sfph/2024-2025-season/my-fair-lady/. The cast in San Francisco Playhouse’s production of My Fair Lady Photo by Jessica Palopoli

articles.text: Piedmont native Tyler Joseph Ellis is starring in the Tony Award-winning musical comedy Shucked, with four weeks of performances scheduled in San Francisco. The show, which The Wall Street Journal calls “flat out hilarious,” will play at the Curran Theatre beginning September 9 with performances through Sunday, October 5, 2025. Tickets for all performances are on sale now at www.broadwaysf.com. The play is set in Cobb County, a town flanked on all sides by the corn fields of Somewhere, America. No one ever goes in or out of Cobb County, content as they are with their daily lives revolving around corn. When the corn fields start dying, however, the town’s way of life is threatened. In the face of this crisis, one brave young woman leaves the town and accidentally enlists the help of a con-man to save her hometown. Chaos and hilarity are sure to ensue. Shucked features a book by Tony Award winner Robert Horn, music by Grammy Award winning country musicians Brandy Clark and Shane McAnally, and directed by three-time Tony Award winner Jack O’Brien. “By the end of my run, I’ll have done it over 300 times,” laughed Ellis about his role in Shucked. Playing the role of Storyteller 2, Ellis acts as the charming narrator. Before he found himself performing eight shows in a week, Ellis got his start in Piedmont schools. He attended Wildwood Elementary School, where every 5th grade class put on a musical. Originally aiming for the role of the Sheriff of Nottingham, Ellis ended up as Robin Hood in the lead role. “It was a profound experience, as a fifth grader,” said Ellis. “I remember being in the bathroom, getting into costume and feeling so nervous but so alive.” Ellis next was in a Piedmont High School production of Oklahoma! in the role of “Slim.” Ellis credits Piedmont School staff with helping him find the passion that would later become his career. “In leaving Piedmont High School, you realize how lucky you had it,” said Ellis. “Piedmont School District and Piedmont High School has such a robust theater culture.” Ellis particularly appreciated PHS Theater Director Kim Taylor’s “state-of-the-art” acting classes and comprehensive theater curriculum. “Piedmont is a rare gift in terms of its focus on the arts, specifically the performing arts. I think the infrastructure, especially for a public school, is sort Tyler Joseph Ellis of unheard-of, and I give so much credit to the faculty and staff that keep it alive,” said Ellis. With his passion for performance ignited, Ellis pursued theater and entertainment wholeheartedly – including his representation of the Pacific Loon in the 50th Annual Leonard J Waxdeck Bird Calling Competition. Ellis graduated from the University of Southern California in 2020 with a major in Theatre and a minor in Marketing. When he’s not on a Broadway tour, his home base is New York City, where he balances a life of comedy content creation, writing, and acting for both stage and screen. Ellis has been featured in co-star roles for the first seasons of HBO Max’s “The Sex Lives of College Girls” and NetPhoto by Matthew Murphy and Evan Zimmerman Maya Lagerstam (left) as Storyteller 1 and Piedmont Native Tyler Joseph Ellis (right) as Storyteller 2 in the North American Tour of Shucked. flix’s “That 90’s Show.” He also co-wrote and starred in the short film “Co-Star,” which has just finished a film festival run and will be available to stream at home soon. One of Ellis’ more nervewracking roles was a July 2023 one-man show titled Tyler’s Quarter-Life Crisis, an autobiographical play about growing up in Piedmont and moving to New York to pursue theater. Ellis is currently writing a new musical comedy with composers Jacob Ryan Smith and Dan Mertzlufft entitled The (Disaster) Marathon of 1904. The show was selected as part of the 2024 New Musicals Lab, and won the third ever Broadway Shark Tank, which gives writers an opportunity to present their shows to a panel of industry judges. “To pursue theater, and to prioritize it in your life, doesn’t need to mean that it’s your entire life,” advised Ellis. “I think there’s a common misconception that if you’re going to be pursuing acting or theater that there is no room for anything else.” For young adults with a passion for acting and theater, Ellis offered some advice. “If you’re feeling it, follow that – because you don’t want to regret not having pursued something that interests you,” said Ellis. “...If you have a strong passion for something, don’t let anyone tell you that’s not worthy of pursuing, in any way, shape or form.” Audiences can see Ellis perform in Shucked for four weeks, September 9-October 5, at the Curran Theater. articles.text: Since the end of WWII, stories of quiet defiance and astonishing bravery have continued to surface, each one reminding us of the resilience of the human spirit. The Courageous Heart of Irena Sendler tells one such story. Set in German-occupied Poland, the film centers on the Warsaw Ghetto, a grim enclosure where 450,000 Jews were forced to live in crushing conditions. From there, families were deported by train, their destinations whispered to be “work camps” but feared to be something far worse — death camps. For many, that possibility was too horrific to grasp. Yet outside the ghetto walls, some refused to look away. Among them was Irena Sendler, a Catholic social worker who disguised herself as a nurse. This guise allowed her to slip past checkpoints, carrying with her not medicine but hope. At staggering personal risk, Irena organized an underground network that smuggled Jewish children out of the ghetto. She used forged papers, hidden exits, tunnels, sewers, even wheelbarrows and trucks. Each journey was fraught with danger, the threat of discovery constant. Perhaps the most heartwrenching task was convincing parents to let go. Irena had to persuade mothers and fathers that entrusting their child to a stranger was the only chance of survival. The weight of those moments — Anna Paquin in The Courageous Heart of Irena Sendler the tears, the fear, the impossible choice — is one of the film’s most powerful threads. Determined to preserve each child’s identity, Irena recorded their names and foster placements on scraps of paper, burying them in jars for safekeeping. She dreamed that parents who survived would one day be reunited with their children. Her mission did not go unnoticed. Near the end of the war she was betrayed to the Gestapo, arrested, and brutally tortured in Warsaw’s notorious Pawiak Prison. Though sentenced to death, she refused to reveal any names. Members of the Polish underground ultimately bribed her guards, and she was freed just before her scheduled execution. She spent the remainder of the war in hiding, continuing her work under a false identity. When the war was over, the true scale of her efforts emerged: 2,500 children rescued. Decades later, in 2007, Irena Sendler was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize — and in real life, she had already been honored in 1965 by Yad Vashem as one of the Righteous Among the Nations, Israel’s recognition of non-Jews who risked everything to save Jews during the Holocaust. The film honors her story with restraint and respect, reminding us that in humanity’s darkest hours, even a single, steadfast heart can make an immeasurable difference. articles.text: Martin Scorsese’s The Irishman is framed by memory and betrayal. At its center is Frank Sheeran (Robert De Niro), a truck driver who becomes a foot soldier for the mob and later a close ally of Teamsters leader Jimmy Hoffa (Al Pacino). The film, drawn from Charles Brandt’s 2004 book I Heard You Paint Houses, traces Sheeran’s life from chance encounter to lifelong entanglement, and finally to isolation in old age. The story opens in a rest home, with a long tracking shot leading to Sheeran in a wheelchair, white-haired and alone, speaking to someone off camera. From there, the narrative unfolds in flashbacks, beginning in the 1950s. Sheeran, hauling meat across Pennsylvania, meets Russell Bufalino (Joe Pesci), a seemingly benign older man who turns out to be a powerful mob boss. That meeting leads to Sheeran’s introduction to Hoffa, a friendship that will shape his life and tether him to the mob-union alliance. The film uses a road trip to Detroit as its spine. Sheeran and Bufalino, traveling with their wives, make stops along the way, each serving as a doorway into memory. These digressions show the mechanics of mob life: loans from the union’s pension fund, favors traded, silence enforced, and the euphemisms that stand in for violence. Sheeran himself becomes a man who “paints houses,” code for killing on command. What emerges is less a riseand-fall story than a study in loyalty and self-deception. Sheeran substitutes the mob for family, giving himself to an organization that promises brotherhood but is, at its core, transactional. articles.text: The children’s classic Black Beauty, written by Anna Swell in 1887, has managed to endure for well over a century, and has been told and retold in books and on the screen. But note that the film I’m recommending in this review was released by Disney+ in 2020 and represents a complete reimagining of the story. Where the original narrative by Sewell is set in Dickensian Victorian England, and Black Beauty is a male mustang (voiced in the 1994 film by Alan Cummings), this most recent release flips the gender of Black Beauty now voiced by Kate Winslet. The story begins in the American West where the young colt (not yet named) roams free with her mother in the Onaqui Mountains of Utah. Free that is until some cowboys round up the wild horses, and in the process separate the youngster from her mother; the two never to be reunited. As it turns out, the young mustang catches the attention of horse trainer John Manley (Iain Glen) who takes her to a horse sanctuary named Birtwick. Though the horse likes Manley, it is nevertheless rebellious and uncooperative, trying the patience of the trainer. At the same time, Manley receives the tragic news that his sister and her husband have been killed in a traffic accident and he is asked to care for his young niece, Jo Green (Mackenzie Foy), Mackenzie Foy in Black Beauty a teenager. Though Jo makes it clear to her uncle that she is unhappy with the situation, and still grieving, the black mustang catches her attention, and wisely Manley puts the difficult horse in the care of Jo, asking her also to work in the stables. As it turns out, the horse (which Jo names Black Beauty) and the teen become close, recognizing that each has suffered an extraordinary loss. And so begins act two. To Jo’s distress, Manley tells her that because Birtwick is in need of money, Black Beauty may have to be sold. articles.text: It was the hottest day of the summer as I pulled into Charles Krug Winery in St. Helena. The old carriage house housed the bottles for the charity auction and the winery tables were arranged around the green lawn under the shade of the old oak trees. This was my second time attending the annual Taste of Mt. Veeder event put on by the Mount Veeder Winery Association and I was excited to revisit some old friends and discover some new wineries. Nature wasn’t making it easy for the wineries to show off their new releases. The wines left out on the table tended to be too warm and the wines pulled from the ice buckets too cold, but the stouthearted vintners pressed on and at the end of the day I was excited to find some really great wines to write about. Mount Veeder is an American Viticultural Area (AVA) among the Mayacaymas Mountains west of Napa and Yountville. The mountain was named after Peter Veeder a Dutch Presbyterian minister who was one of the first non-natives to explore the area. The area has been producing wines since the 1860’s and is the only hillside appellation in Napa Valley that adjoins the cool, bayside Carneros, benefiting from the cooling influence of San Pablo Bay. Mount Veeder is an island of ancient seabed pushed up into a mountain surrounded by volcanic soils that typify the rest of Napa Valley. The rugged mountain terrain of extremely steep slopes above the fog, renders shallow topsoil and minimal water retention, resulting in tiny berries with intense flavor and concentration. The Mount Veeder AVA is small with only about 35 wineries producing 40,000 cases per vintage or about 1.3% of total Napa Valley production. This year’s Taste of Mt. Veeder event featured 26 wineries pouring their new releases. The following wines were the cream of the crop – the best of Mt. Veeder. • 2021 Yates Family Fleur de Veeder $80 Coming from a vineyard that has been continuously farmed since 1880 the Yates Family Merlot has an earthy nose with herbal notions over a core of cassis, plums and blackberries with hints of cedar and menthol. Quite mineral in the medium-bodied mouth it has soft tannins and just enough freshness, finishing long and earthy. Great job. • 2021 Mi Sueno Cabernet Sauvignon Lynne’s Vineyard $105 The deep garnet colored Mi Sueno Cabernet sashays out of the glass with provocative warm blueberry and raspberry scents with an undercurrent of violets and forest floor. The full-bodied palate is laden with fragrant black and blue fruits, framed by firm, finely grained tannins and seamless freshness, finishing long and perfumed. This wine should improve for up to two decades in the cellar. • 2022 Robert Craig Cabernet Franc Amenet Vineyard $118 Cabernet Franc is a grape that requires lots of sun to avoid being vegetal and Robert Craig has found the right spot on Mt. Veeder. The wine shows beautiful blueberry and cassis fruit, a cool, almost floral note, medium to full body and sensational purity and texture found in this big boned classic mountain wine. This is a beauty of finesse and restraint, yet intensity. Drink over the next 25 years. • 2023 Baker Canyon Cabernet Sauvignon $250 Only 300 cases of the wine were produced by this new winery at the northern tip of the Mt. Veeder appellation. The Baker Canyon Cab possesses an uncommonly dense black/purple color, and a sweet nose of licorice, underbrush, blackcurrants and toast. Amazingly extracted, yet somehow retaining its elegance, this wine offers the essence of black fruits in its long, rich, full-bodied flavors. There are Baker Canyon Winery is a new winery on Mt. articles.text: Among those participating in Wednesday’s Walk were Carolyn George, Ken Moy, Alissa Quan, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Brenda Ferrero, Alicia Rivera, Karen Palmer, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Irene Thompson, Mark Davis, Tina Shum, Judy Love, Phil Witte, Stella Houston, Greg Slattoff, Peggy Shultz, Greg Keller, Pat Keller, Sherry Jacobs, Bonnie Sherwood with K-9 best friend Zippy, Mary Ann Barnes, Lori Austin, Helen Dong, Dave DeRoche, Mary Carter, Noemi Alvarado, Bill Ahern, Dan Scdoris, Albert Chen, Edith Lee, June Yee, and Dick Carter. The Walking on Wednesdays group had a good turnout of about 40 walkers and four K-9 best friends at the Exedra last Wednesday for their weekly walk. The City of Piedmont re-opened the Linda Pickleball courts in early August after resurfacing and marking them exclusively for pickleball. The courts are closed on Wednesdays so the walkers could inspect the courts without interrupting anyone’s play. Piedmont Recreation Department’s Liam Kelly was to meet them at the courts. The group went down Magnolia and up to the seldom traveled MacKinnon Place, a culde-sac. A hidden 110-foot set of about 48 steep stairs took them down to Arbor Drive. The group went up to Oakland Avenue and went down to Linda Avenue wot see the newly resurfaced pickleball courts. Liam Kelly asked the walkers if they could remember what the space had previously been used for. Dick Carter remembered playing softball on it as an elementary school student in the late 1950s. The site had also been basketball courts and most recently a pair of undersized tennis courts. The project was initially funded to be completed in 2023, and the popularity of pickleball exploded. Trials were conducted and temporary courts were set up at different locations, but the demand for pickleball was evident. How this demand could be met became a controversial issue. The Piedmont Recreation Commission made a recommendation to the City Council that the Linda Tennis Courts be converted into pickleball courts. This led to a lawsuit from neighbors who cited concerns about the noise associated with pickleball play and the impact on nearby residents. Accommodations and sound mitigation efforts have been made. The courts are open from 9 to 6 weekdays, 9 to 3 on Sundays, and closed on Wednesdays. There are no lights. Low-noise balls are provided in a large bin and there is a list of low noise rackets at the courts. There are no reservations needed and there are no fees. The Piedmont Public Works Department began the $60,000 project to reconstruct, resurface, and restripe the Linda Pickleball Courts in April. The project was originally expected to take two months, but there were delays in receiving court equipment. In addition, two trees whose roots were causing uneven court surfaces had to be removed. The transformation was a challenge, but the result is impressive. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: So, it’s fall, 1959, and when you walk into your staid New England prep school English class for the first time, your teacher asks you to stand on your desk. You do. It’s both exhilarating and alarming. Is this higher learning? What in the world could come next? High school junior Todd Anderson finds out fast from John Keating, a new addition to the faculty, who, when he himself was a student there years ago, belonged to something called “The Dead Poets Society.” One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what the Piedmont Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting, and then a lively discussion of it afterward. This month’s selection is 1989’s Dead Poet’s Society, directed by Peter Weir and starring Robin Williams as the unorthodox teacher, Keating, and Ethan Hawke as his student, Todd. The school, Welton Academy, is an all-boys prep school known for its ancient traditions and high standards. A breath of fresh air, Keating uses unorthodox methods to reach out to the teenage boys, who face enormous pressures from their parents and the school. With Keating’s help, students Todd Anderson, his friend Neil Perry (Robert Sean Leonard) and others learn to break out of their shells, pursue their dreams and seize the day. The film received mixed reviews from critics, but it’s been an audience favorite for years. Attendees polled by CinemaScore gave the film a rare “A+” grade. Time Magazine said, “Williams, who has comparatively little screen time, has come to act, not to cut comic riffs, and he does so with forceful, ultimately compelling, simplicity,” and Pauline Kale said, “Robin Williams’ performance is more graceful than anything he’s done before. He’s totally, concentratedly here. He reads his lines stunningly, and when he mimics various actors reciting Shakespeare, there’s no undue clowning in it; he’s a gifted teacher demonstrating his skills.” Dead Poet’s Society will be screened on September 11 at the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 1:00 p.m. Sponsored by the Rec Department, the film series continues on the second Thursday of each month. Doors will open at 12:45. The event is free and available to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP is encouraged. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch.

articles.text: Organizations that provide adult recreational activities inside the city of Piedmont are invited to participate in the second annual Piedmont Adult Recreation EXPO. The EXPO will be held on Sunday, November 16, from 2:00 to 4:00 p.m. at the Piedmont Veterans Memorial Building, 401 Highland Avenue. This event will showcase recreational programs from the Piedmont Recreation Department, the Piedmont Adult School, the Piedmont Center for the Arts, and other organizations. Representatives will table at the event and explain to attendees how they can get involved in the different groups’ fall 2025 and winter 2026 recreational programs, activities, or classes. There is no fee to participate in or attend the EXPO. The event will be open to all adults, Piedmont residents and non-residents. Last year’s EXPO in November was highly successful with approximately 200 people participating. This community service event is being conducted by Piedmont volunteers. The event is supported by the Piedmont Recreation Department, the Piedmont Adult School, the Piedmont Center for the Arts, and a limited number of corporate sponsors. In 2023 an Older Adult Recreation Report concluded that there was a broad range of recreational opportunities available for older adults in Piedmont from many organizations, however people often were unaware of them or did not know how to get involved. The EXPO addresses this opportunity and increases adult participation in Piedmont recreation of many different types. Groups that provide recreation for adults within the city of Piedmont and want to participate in the EXPO should contact Lisa Gardner at lgardner555@gmail. com or Dick Carter camktgrp@ comcast.net to register or get more info. Patty Dunlap (right) the President of the Piedmont Beautification Foundation talks about the group during last year’s Expo. Last year’s Piedmont Adult Recreation Expo in Veteran’s Hall

articles.text: Noticing grey hairs on your furry friend’s muzzle? It could be time to switch up your care routine to better support the needs of an aging dog. While we can’t make them live forever, implementing a few key changes can help extend your canine companion’s golden years. This goes beyond just slowing down on walks; their medical and nutritional needs require some increased attention at this stage of life too. Be sure to consult with your vet to determine the best care for your senior pup. When your dog shows signs of aging, consider adjusting their diet. The Shallows is a taut thriller, absent any dialogue to speak of. What that means is that all that is emotive about this nicely drawn film depends on the considerable ability of Lively, who must now endure a long, cold night while ever aware that with the arrival of high tide in the morning her place on the rock will gradually become more and more precarious. Being in the water, even the shallows, will mean all but certain death. As the sun sets she waits and shivers in the dark and grimaces from the pain of not only her severe leg injury, but countless coral cuts and abrasions. Lively’s performance is spot-on as the camera tightly follows her tenacious attempt at resisting a mind numbing panic, fighting to be resourceful and brave. Her expressions, the clench of her jaw, the look in her eyes, the pep talks she gives herself saturates her situation with an abiding verisimilitude. The role also required a tour de force of demanding athleticism. Clearly, The Shallows is an adrenaline-inducing movie that will grip you from the moment you reach for that first handful of popcorn until the end credits.
